cases.title: Fold a constant projection
cases.note: The multiplication in the output becomes a constant value. Compare the Project expression before and after the rule.

input.sql: SELECT name, 10 * 20 AS threshold FROM customers

cases.title: Fold a constant in a predicate
cases.note: The amount threshold is evaluated inside the filter expression.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id > 10 * 20

cases.title: Push an order filter into a join input
cases.note: The amount predicate references only orders, allowing it to move below the inner join.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount > 100

cases.title: Push a filter through a projection
cases.note: The next_id alias is replaced with its input expression when the filter moves below Project.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM (SELECT name, id + 1 AS next_id FROM customers) t WHERE next_id > 10

cases.title: Prune unused join input columns
cases.note: Input projections retain the requested output and columns needed for the join. This is logical pruning, not measured storage savings.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

cases.title: Remove an identity projection
cases.note: A projection that preserves every input field can be removed.

input.sql: SELECT * FROM customers

cases.title: Rewrite a join as a correlate
cases.note: The join is rewritten using a correlated input and corresponding predicates.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount > 100

cases.title: Extract an inner join condition
cases.note: The inner join condition moves into a separate filter above a Cartesian join.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount > 100

cases.title: Push a condition from inside a join
cases.note: A condition that references only the orders input can move out of the inner join condition.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.amount > 100

cases.title: Simplify a join expression
cases.note: Constant arithmetic in the join condition is reduced.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.amount > 50 + 50

cases.title: Represent a filter as Calc
cases.note: Calc combines projection and filtering in an expression program. This change does not execute the query.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id > 10

cases.title: Represent a projection as Calc
cases.note: The projection is represented as a Calc expression program.

input.sql: SELECT name, id + 1 AS next_id FROM customers

cases.title: Move projection below a filter
cases.note: A projection is placed below the filter while retaining fields required by the predicate.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id > 10

cases.title: Expand an average aggregate
cases.note: AVG is expressed using simpler aggregates and a final expression, preserving Calcite type and NULL semantics.

input.sql: SELECT customer_id, AVG(amount) AS average_amount FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

cases.title: Expand a distinct aggregate
cases.note: Distinct aggregation is rewritten into relational operators that isolate duplicate elimination.

input.sql: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(DISTINCT amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

cases.title: Merge an aggregate input projection
cases.note: The aggregate uses the underlying input fields directly when the projection can be absorbed.

input.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

cases.title: Convert conditional aggregation to a filter
cases.note: A CASE expression used by an aggregate becomes an aggregate filter when its semantics allow it.

input.sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN amount > 100 THEN amount ELSE NULL END) FROM orders

cases.title: Push aggregation into union inputs
cases.note: Partial aggregates are computed below UNION ALL and combined above it.

input.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM (SELECT customer_id, amount FROM orders UNION ALL SELECT customer_id, amount FROM orders) t GROUP BY customer_id

cases.title: Move sorting through a projection
cases.note: The sort and projection are reordered while preserving ordering semantics.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers ORDER BY name

cases.title: Separate union and duplicate removal
cases.note: A distinct UNION becomes UNION ALL followed by duplicate elimination.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers UNION SELECT city FROM customers

cases.title: Expand an intersection
cases.note: INTERSECT is expressed using aggregation and filtering while preserving distinct semantics.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers INTERSECT SELECT city FROM customers

cases.title: Expand a set difference
cases.note: EXCEPT is rewritten into relational operators that preserve set difference semantics.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers EXCEPT SELECT city FROM customers

cases.title: Filter literal rows
cases.note: A filter over literal rows is evaluated and merged into Values.

input.sql: SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1), (2), (3)) AS t(id) WHERE id > 1

cases.title: Project literal rows
cases.note: Expressions over literal rows are evaluated into new Values rows.

input.sql: SELECT id + 1 FROM (VALUES (1), (2)) AS t(id)

cases.title: Remove a zero-row fetch
cases.note: A fetch limit of zero allows the subtree to be replaced by an empty result.

input.sql: SELECT * FROM customers FETCH NEXT 0 ROWS ONLY

cases.title: Simplify a join with one literal row
cases.note: A one-row Values input can be replaced with equivalent expressions and filters.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM (VALUES (1)) AS v(id) JOIN customers c ON v.id = c.id

cases.title: Remove a proven constant grouping key
cases.note: Constant metadata allows the rule to remove a grouping key even without requiring a Project operand.

input.sql: SELECT city, k, COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT city, 1 AS k FROM customers) t GROUP BY city,k

cases.title: Expand distinct aggregates using joins
cases.note: Separate distinct inputs are aggregated and combined by a join.

input.sql: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(DISTINCT amount), SUM(DISTINCT id) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

cases.title: Expand aggregation with distinct keys
cases.note: WITHIN DISTINCT is expanded into grouped relational operators after SUM normalization. This example describes a plan; runtime uniqueness checks are not executed.

input.sql: SELECT customer_id,SUM(amount),SUM(amount) WITHIN DISTINCT (id) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

cases.title: Move aggregation below a filter
cases.note: Aggregation moves below the filter while retaining the columns needed to evaluate its predicate.

input.sql: SELECT city,COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE id>10 GROUP BY city

cases.title: Remove an unused nested outer join
cases.note: Distinct aggregation makes an intermediate outer join redundant when its fields are not needed.

input.sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id LEFT JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

cases.title: Remove an outer join below distinct aggregation
cases.note: Duplicate elimination on the preserved input makes the unused side of the outer join unnecessary.

input.sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id

cases.title: Push partial aggregation below a join
cases.note: Partial sums are placed on join inputs and combined above the join. No data is executed or performance gain measured.

input.sql: SELECT c.city,SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id GROUP BY c.city

cases.title: Combine nested aggregates
cases.note: The upper SUM of counts is combined with the lower aggregation at the coarser grouping level.

input.sql: SELECT city, SUM(n) FROM (SELECT city,name,COUNT(*) n FROM customers GROUP BY city,name) t GROUP BY city

cases.title: Remove a constant grouping key
cases.note: The constant grouping key is pulled above the aggregate and restored in the output projection.

input.sql: SELECT city, k, COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT city, 1 AS k FROM customers) t GROUP BY city,k

cases.title: Remove aggregation over unique literal rows
cases.note: The literal input has distinct grouping keys, so MIN can be replaced by the corresponding input expression.

input.sql: SELECT id,MIN(id) FROM (VALUES (1),(2)) t(id) GROUP BY id

cases.title: Remove redundant union-input aggregation
cases.note: The outer distinct aggregate makes a duplicate-eliminating aggregate inside UNION ALL redundant.

input.sql: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM (SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers) t

cases.title: Remove aggregation from the first union input
cases.note: The outer distinct aggregate makes the duplicate-eliminating aggregate in the first UNION ALL input redundant.

input.sql: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM (SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers) t

cases.title: Remove aggregation from the second union input
cases.note: The outer distinct aggregate makes the duplicate-eliminating aggregate in the second UNION ALL input redundant.

input.sql: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM (SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers) t

cases.title: Evaluate aggregation over an empty input
cases.note: Preparation exposes empty Values. The selected rule produces the aggregate result prescribed for empty input.

input.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE 1=0

cases.title: Merge adjacent Calc programs
cases.note: The filter and projection are first represented as separate Calc programs. The selected rule combines those programs.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id>10

cases.title: Lower decimal arithmetic in Calc
cases.note: Decimal multiplication in a Calc program is rewritten using primitive numeric operations and scale adjustments.

input.sql: SELECT amount * 1.20 FROM orders

cases.title: Fold a constant in Calc
cases.note: After projection-to-Calc conversion, the multiplication in the expression program becomes a literal.

input.sql: SELECT name,10*20 AS threshold FROM customers

cases.title: Remove an identity Calc
cases.note: An identity projection is first represented as Calc. The selected rule removes that redundant program.

input.sql: SELECT * FROM customers

cases.title: Split Calc into relational operators
cases.note: The prepared Calc program is split into projection and filtering operators.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id>10

cases.title: Extract a window from Calc
cases.note: The prepared Calc contains a window expression. The selected rule extracts it into a Window operator.

input.sql: SELECT name,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY id) rn FROM customers

cases.title: Push a grouping-key predicate below aggregation
cases.note: The HAVING condition references only a grouping key and can be evaluated before aggregation.

input.sql: SELECT city,COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY city HAVING city='London'

cases.title: Merge a filter into Calc
cases.note: The input projection is first represented as Calc. The filter condition is then incorporated into that program.

input.sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT id+1 AS id,name FROM customers) t WHERE id>10

cases.title: Push a filter through Correlate
cases.note: A join is first represented as Correlate. The selected rule moves eligible predicates to its inputs.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount>10

cases.title: Push a filter into an inner join
cases.note: The non-smart variant moves eligible predicates into the join inputs without applying the smart outer-join simplification.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount>100

cases.title: Combine adjacent filters
cases.note: Removing identity projections exposes two filters; the selected rule combines their predicates.

input.sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id>10) t WHERE id<20

cases.title: Attach a filter to MultiJoin
cases.note: The join tree is first represented as MultiJoin. The selected rule incorporates the filter into that representation.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount>10

cases.title: Move a filter below sampling
cases.note: The filter and sampling operators are reordered by the selected Calcite rule. Sample outcomes are not evaluated.

input.sql: SELECT * FROM customers TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI(20) WHERE id>10

cases.title: Push a filter into set-operation inputs
cases.note: The same predicate is evaluated on the inputs of UNION ALL.

input.sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT id,name FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT id,name FROM customers) t WHERE id>10

cases.title: Expand a filter subquery
cases.note: SQL conversion preserves the IN subquery so that the selected rule can produce its relational rewrite.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)

cases.title: Push a partition-key filter below Window
cases.note: Window extraction and filter transposition expose the Window. The city predicate keeps whole partitions and can move below it.

input.sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT id,city,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY id) rn FROM customers) t WHERE city='London'

cases.title: Rebuild joins from a hypergraph
cases.note: After hypergraph construction, Calcite’s experimental join reordering rule produces a join tree. Estimates use schema-only metadata.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

cases.title: Flatten nested intersections
cases.note: Nested intersections are combined into a single set operation with more inputs.

input.sql: (SELECT name FROM customers INTERSECT SELECT city FROM customers) INTERSECT SELECT name FROM customers

cases.title: Introduce a redundant semijoin
cases.note: An additional semijoin is introduced as an optimizer candidate. The demonstration stops after one match and does not claim a cheaper plan.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

cases.title: Regroup a three-input join
cases.note: The left-nested join is rewritten as a right-nested join with adjusted predicates. One match is shown.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

cases.title: Swap inner-join inputs
cases.note: The join inputs are swapped and a projection preserves the original output order. A one-match limit prevents repeated swaps.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

cases.title: Swap join inputs with the outer-capable variant
cases.note: This variant permits outer joins as well as inner joins. The bounded example shows one input swap and preserves output order.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

cases.title: Infer non-null join inputs
cases.note: Equality in an inner join allows non-null predicates to be inferred for nullable join keys.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

cases.title: Distribute a join over its left union input
cases.note: The join is applied to each UNION ALL branch on the left.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT * FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT * FROM customers) c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id

cases.title: Use a semijoin with a unique right input
cases.note: The right literal keys are unique and only left-side fields are projected, allowing a semijoin rewrite.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN (VALUES (1),(2)) v(id) ON c.id=v.id

cases.note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the outer join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT id+1 AS id,name FROM customers) c LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id+1 AS customer_id,amount FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

cases.title: Pull left input projections above a join
cases.note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the inner join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT id+1 AS id,name FROM customers) c INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id

cases.title: Pull left input projections above a join
cases.note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the outer join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM (SELECT id+1 AS id,name FROM customers) c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id

cases.title: Pull right input projections above a join
cases.note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the inner join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c INNER JOIN (SELECT customer_id+1 AS customer_id,amount FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

cases.title: Pull right input projections above a join
cases.note: Computed join-input projections are pulled above the outer join, with field references rewritten to preserve the result.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id+1 AS customer_id,amount FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

cases.note: A range predicate on one order input is propagated to the other input through equality of their nullable customer IDs.

input.sql: SELECT a.id FROM (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id > 10) a JOIN orders b ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id

cases.title: Distribute a join over its right union input
cases.note: The join is applied to each UNION ALL branch on the right.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN (SELECT * FROM orders UNION ALL SELECT * FROM orders) o ON c.id=o.customer_id

cases.title: Expand a subquery in a join condition
cases.note: SQL conversion preserves the aggregate subquery in the join condition for the selected rule to rewrite.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id AND o.amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders)

cases.note: The join tree becomes Calcite’s experimental HyperGraph representation.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

cases.title: Flatten a join tree into MultiJoin
cases.note: The binary join tree becomes a MultiJoin representation for subsequent join-order rules.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

cases.note: After flattening and recording projected fields, the rule constructs a join tree using Calcite’s heuristic ordering.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

cases.title: Construct a bushy join tree
cases.note: The prepared MultiJoin is converted into a potentially bushy join tree. No real statistics or runtime cost measurements are supplied.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN orders p ON c.id=p.customer_id

cases.note: The outer projection does not use COUNT, allowing the aggregate call to be removed while retaining grouping.

cases.note: The filter is first converted to Calc. The output projection is then incorporated into that program.

input.sql: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id>10

cases.note: A join is first represented as Correlate. Projections retain output columns and required correlation fields.

input.sql: SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id

cases.note: Both projection and predicate expressions are considered as whole expressions during transposition.

cases.note: The computed output expression moves below Filter, with fields needed by the predicate retained.

cases.note: The join tree is flattened first. The projection then records which MultiJoin fields are required.

cases.note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the join left operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.

cases.note: Preparation proves an input empty. The selected pruning rule rewrites the join right operation while preserving its empty-input and outer-join semantics.
